tagline.text: Lucban's May harvest thanksgiving, with houses dressed in kiping

location.label: Location
location.text: Downtown Lucban, Quezon (around the Saint Isidore the Farmer Parish Church)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱800–2,500 (meals, transport and snacks, rough estimate for a day trip)

children.text: The Pahiyas Festival is a harvest thanksgiving held every May 15 in Lucban, Quezon, in honor of San Isidro Labrador, the patron saint of farmers. House after house is decorated with colorful rice wafers called kiping, vegetables and fruit, and in the afternoon a procession of the saint passes through the streets.

The Pahiyas Festival is a harvest thanksgiving held every year on May 15 in Lucban, Quezon. It honors San Isidro Labrador, regarded as the patron saint of farmers, and gives thanks for the blessings of the year's farming. Among the Philippines' May festivals it is one of the most colorful, and it draws local and foreign photographers alike.

The heart of the festival is the house decorations. Houses along the main streets and alleys of town cover their facades with kiping, freshly harvested vegetables, fruit, rice stalks, bamboo crafts and wooden ornaments. Kiping are thin, leaf-shaped wafers made from glutinous rice and dyed in bright colors, and you can grill or fry them and dip them in vinegar. A 2024 news report described a house covered entirely in chayote and cabbage and another with an image of San Isidro made of mung beans, corn and palay (rice). Local media also report that in some years residents saved money by using more real produce instead of kiping. That is why the colors and materials of the houses differ from year to year, and watching those changes is part of the fun.

The modern festival is described as having been organized in 1963 by Fernando Cadeliña Nañawa, then president of Lucban's Art Club, based on older traditions. Stories say that before Spanish rule, farmers carried their harvests to the foothills of Mount Banahaw to have them blessed, and that after colonization the ritual moved into the church. Later, harvests were displayed outside homes and the priest went from house to house to bless them, an account that leads to the festival's present form.

The festival could not be held during the pandemic and returned in 2022, and in 2024 there were reports that more houses were decorated than in recent years. How lavish the decorations are varies from year to year and can be simpler when times are tight. Dates and programs change a little every year, so check the latest announcements. The festival is also a time when Lucban natives living elsewhere come home, so each house fills with relatives and guests sharing food, with an atmosphere like a family holiday.

Ordinary homes, shops and even government offices decorate their facades with kiping and farm produce. Even with the same kiping, the patterns and color combinations differ from house to house, so you will not get bored walking a single block. Neighbors help each other decorate, and there is reportedly a competition with a prize for the best-decorated house.

On the afternoon of May 15, a procession of San Isidro statues passes through town. Descriptions mention statues depicting different stages of the saint's life, giant papier-mâché puppets called higantes, a marching band and folk performers. The timing and route change a little every year, so confirm locally.

blocks.title: Around the Saint Isidore the Farmer Parish Church

children.text: The center of the event is the area around Lucban's Spanish-era church, where decorated houses cluster along streets such as Gomburza, La Purisima Concepcion, Lopez Jaena, Gregorio del Pilar and Mabini. Use the road in front of the church as your reference point as you walk.

Pancit habhab, a Quezon specialty, is a noodle snack served on a banana leaf and eaten by hand. One reviewer reported finding free servings at nearly every street corner during the festival. Judge the hygiene and the waiting time for yourself.

Local foods such as Lucban longganisa (sausage), kesong puti (white cheese), espasol (rice cake), pilipit kalabasa and hardinera sell most during this period. Some households invite visitors into their homes to share a feast.

During the festival there is reportedly a night market selling local products, a food market and evening concerts. If you are tired from walking in the daytime, relax at the evening show and the market.

blocks.title: Impromptu performances and the carabao parade

children.text: Outside the scheduled times, small parades and carabao (water buffalo) processions can pop up without notice. Keep your camera ready at all times.

Events honoring the same saint are held under different names in many Quezon towns, including Agawan in Sariaya, Arañat Baluarte in Gumaca, Anihan in Mauban and Mayohan in Tayabas. If Lucban is too crowded, a neighboring town is worth considering.

items.title: Day trip from Manila
items.subtitle: Leave at dawn and watch the afternoon procession

children.text: Head from Manila (or its outskirts) to a bus terminal for Lucena, Quezon. Roads are jammed on festival day, so an early start is safer.
Transfer in Lucena to a jeepney or van to Lucban. On festival day, entry into town may be restricted, so follow the instructions.
Walk in from the edge of town toward the Saint Isidore the Farmer Parish Church. In the morning it is still relatively uncrowded and the soft light makes for good photos.
Tour Gomburza, Lopez Jaena and Mabini streets to admire the house decorations and taste pancit habhab and kiping.
After lunch, find a spot along the route of the San Isidro procession.
Start heading home before dark. To avoid the rush of departing crowds, move a little earlier.

A day trip takes a lot of energy. Bring a hat, water and comfortable shoes, and rest in the shade during the scorching sun from 12:00 to 15:00. In the strong midday sun, rest inside the church or in a shaded restaurant and save your energy for the afternoon procession. In crowded spots, agree on a meeting place with your group in advance.

items.title: Overnight trip
items.subtitle: Arrive the day before and see the preparations

children.text: Arrive in Lucban or Lucena the day before the festival and find a room. Rooms fill up early just before May 15.
You can reportedly see people preparing house decorations even the day before. Stroll slowly and watch the decorating.
On festival day, go into town early and enjoy the quiet morning decorations.
After watching the afternoon procession, enjoy the evening show and the night market.
The next morning, buy souvenirs such as Lucban sausage or kiping and head back to Manila.

The festival is held every year on May 15. May is the hottest time of year in the Philippines, with high daytime temperatures and strong sun. A good rhythm is to arrive in the early morning and see the house decorations first, rest in the shade or indoors at midday, then come back out for the afternoon procession.
News reports say the government has declared May 15 a special non-working day in Lucban. Book accommodation and transport about a month ahead.

On festival day, the mood of the street flows in this order: admiring decorations in the morning, a break at noon, the procession in the afternoon and a show in the evening. To see everything in a single day, plan your timetable around this order.

Lucban town has few places to stay, so rooms vanish early around the festival. A common approach is to stay in Lucena and travel in the morning, and many people come from Manila as a day trip. Check exact room prices and availability by date on booking sites.

Food is half of this trip. Pancit habhab is the basic, and Lucban longganisa is a rich, garlicky sausage. Kiping turns into a crisp snack when grilled, so try buying a single piece. Check the hygiene of street food yourself and drink plenty of water.

The kiping used for house decorations is originally a food that carries the meaning of thanks for the harvest. Along the festival streets, you can buy packaged kiping from the households or shops that make it as a souvenir. It breaks easily, so carry it in a hard box, and the unfried kind is usually grilled or fried before eating. Before eating, check that it has not absorbed moisture.

Bring a hat, sunscreen, water, a thin long-sleeved layer and comfortable sneakers. It is very hot in the daytime.
To guard against phone snatching, wear your bag in front and keep cash in separate places.
When taking photos close to a house's decorations, politely ask the owner first.
Kiping is a decorative material but also an edible snack, so you can buy some separately where it is sold.
Procession times and routes differ every year, so check local notices or local government announcements.
Toilets are limited, so use the restaurants or shops near the church beforehand.
Many police are deployed, so follow instructions and keep behind barriers.
If you touch decorations after taking a photo, ask the owner's permission. Kiping breaks easily.
Lucban is extremely crowded on festival day. Prepare for traffic closures, heat and pickpockets, and decide on your way home in advance.
Roads may be closed and you may have to walk far, so allow plenty of time.
The daytime heat in May can cause dehydration or heatstroke, so drink water often and rest in the shade.
During the procession, do not get too close to the statues and participants, and follow instructions.
Book accommodation and transport early, and expect prices to rise.
The festival schedule and the format of the procession may change from year to year, so check official announcements just before you go.
